headline: 116, 117 and 118 differ from 108-115, but each in different ways: Task 2 (base rate, label validity) breaks in 116-117 and partly reverts in 118, while Task 1 (positive density) breaks only in 118. So the two candidate test Congresses (117 for S1a, 118 for S1b) are off-distribution for different tasks. Section A therefore argues for a forward split that is evaluated per task and per Congress, with base-rate- and density-aware metrics. It does not single out one val/test pair as clean.
overview:
Section A asks whether what a model learns from (labels, features, and the label-feature relationship) stays stable from the training Congresses (108-115) to the candidate validation/test Congresses (116, 117, 118). Each candidate is judged against a 95% *t prediction interval*: the range one new Congress should fall in if nothing changed. The interval is built from only 6-8 reference Congresses (8 for most checks, 7 for A18, 6 for the forward-chained A12/A13/A18b), so it is wide, about +/-2.5 to 2.8 times the between-Congress SD. A check fails only if a test survives a Holm multiple-comparison correction. Holm-surviving failures are strong evidence, but their p-values are approximate. Some failures rest only on the *joint* test, which compares the mean of the three candidates with the reference Congresses and treats 116, 117 and 118 as independent draws. They are consecutive and probably autocorrelated, so those joint p-values are anti-conservative. In the other direction, a pass often means *not detectable with n = 6-8*, not *stable*.

**Which Congress shifts in what** (Holm survivors; "joint only" = no single cell survives):
- **116:** label validity (A1b, cell), House Task-2 rate (A2, joint only), bill volume (A8), Task-2 AUROC (A13: t0-safe part by cell, full part joint only). Task-1 density and original share are normal.
- **117:** everything 116 has, plus original-cosponsor share (A4). It has the lowest Task-2 rate in the series (2.81%; raw failure of A1, not Holm-surviving). Task-1 density is low but inside the interval (t = -2.0).
- **118:** Task-1 density (A3, cells at t0 = 0 and 7), original share (A4), volume (A8), Task-2 AUROC (A13, joint only). Its Task-2 rate (4.41%), label-miss share (0.473) and House rate are back inside the train spread.

Only volume and A13 fail in all three. The cluster test A17 rejects chance for each candidate (p = 0.005, <0.001 and 0.044).

**What the shifts look like.** Task-2 rate: pooled 6.5% in train against 4.14% / 2.81% / 4.41%. In 116 and 118 most of the drop comes from a bigger denominator (law-capable volume 1.32x and 1.54x the mean train Congress), not from fewer reported bills. The exception is 117, where fewer reports dominate. In 116-117, 58-61% of chamber-passed bills have no committee report within 180 days, against 35-53% in train, so the label captures less of real advancement. Task-1 density in 118 is 0.47% at t0 = 0, about 40% below the train mean (about 0.80%). The number of new day-1-30 cosponsorships in 118 is normal, so this looks mainly like a normal number of joiners spread over many more bills.

**What held.** The bill-feature mix is no more shifted than train Congresses are from each other (A7, A9, A11). For Task 1, a simple pair model (5 features, t0 = 7 only) fitted on earlier Congresses discriminates at or above its train level on 116-118, with calibration slope near 1 (A18b). This is pair-level AUROC, not per-bill Recall@K/NDCG. The majority-sponsor effect differs strongly by controlling party within train (A5c). Regime explains part of its 116-117 dip, but all three House candidates still sit below their own regime's reference.

**Inference for the split.** All of these are differences between history and the period the model will be used in. Forward splits measure them (S1a and S1a+stream fail 6 of 20 judged checks, the others 7, because they also evaluate 118). The random split S5 cannot see them. Section A barely discriminates between forward splits on counts. Its main message for the val/test choice is that S1a tests Task 2 on its most anomalous Congress (117), while S1b *validates* Task 2 on 117 and tests Task 1 on its most anomalous Congress (118). Results should therefore be reported per task and per Congress, and any tuning or recalibration on a single val Congress should be checked out of sample.

A-c9-txt.interpretation: Setup for section A. The reference pool is 108-115 and the candidates are 116, 117 and 118. There are 110,802 uncensored advancement labels (censored = not yet followed for the full 180 days), and 47 bill-level features over 128,791 law-capable bills. Both chambers of the 119th are Republican-controlled, which matters for the regime comparisons in A15. A handful of bills (at most 11, in 117) have a sponsor with no caucus/party assignment.
A-c9-txt.caveats: These 11 bills in 117 later drive the top domain-classifier coefficient for 117 (sponsor_caucus=(missing), +3.10 log-odds) in A11. With so few bills this is plausibly a data-coding effect rather than substantive drift.

A-c11-txt.interpretation: The Task-2 positive rate per Congress is 4.3-8.7% in train (pooled 6.5%), against 4.14% (116), 2.81% (117) and 4.41% (118). Only 117 falls outside the prediction interval [3.29%, 12.19%] (t = -2.9). The joint test that all three sit low is nominally significant (t = -3.0, p = 0.02), but nothing survives Holm, so A1 is recorded as PASS. The decomposition is the informative part. Reported-bill counts in 116 and 118 are normal (491 and 611 vs a train range of 414-839; A1d PASS), and bill volume is 1.32-1.54x the mean train Congress. Volume explains 61% of the log drop in 116 and all of it in 118. In 117, fewer reports explain the larger share (count part -0.476 vs volume part -0.362, volume share 0.43). So 118 is near the train spread (t = -1.3), and 117 is the real Task-2 base-rate outlier.
A-c11-txt.caveats: PASS here is a power statement. With 8 reference Congresses the interval spans almost a factor of 4 in rate, and the candidates are three of the four lowest values (only 112, at 4.32%, is below 118). Chi-square p-values are uninformative at about 10k bills per Congress. Rates are computed on uncensored bills only, and candidates have higher censored shares (15.0-17.3% vs 9.6-15.2% in train). If late-introduced bills differ systematically in their reporting odds, the candidate rates carry a selection effect that the notebook does not quantify.

A-c13-txt.interpretation: A1b measures how much real advancement the label misses. Among bills that passed their chamber of origin within 180 days, the share without a committee report within 180 days is 60.5% in 116 and 58.1% in 117, against 34.7-52.6% in train. 116 survives Holm on its own, and so does the joint test (t = +3.0, p = 0.0095). Both are labelled breaks. 118 is back at 47.3% (t = +0.7), inside the train spread. So the label-validity problem is specific to 116-117, not a growing trend. In those two Congresses the label captures a smaller fraction of bills that actually advance, plausibly via suspension of the rules or unanimous consent, though the notebook does not test those routes directly. Under the alternative label (reported OR passed origin chamber), the 116 and 117 drops shrink (log ratio -0.451 to -0.272 and -0.838 to -0.558), but in 118 the drop grows slightly (-0.387 to -0.469).
A-c13-txt.caveats: The joint test pools 116-118 as independent draws. 116 and 117 are consecutive and share a House-D majority, so its p-value is optimistic. The 116 cell result does not depend on that assumption. The alternative label still trends down (joint t = -2.6, p = 0.038, not Holm-surviving), so part of the base-rate drop is a label artifact, but not all of it. Passed-bill counts are small (353-787 per Congress), so unrep_share is noisy, and the chamber splits rest on even fewer bills.

A-c15-txt.interpretation: By chamber, the drop is a House phenomenon concentrated in 116-117. House rates are 3.51% and 2.57% there, against 4.59-9.05% in train (t = -2.4 and -3.6, both labelled breaks). 118's House rate (4.29%, t = -1.6) is inside the interval. No House cell survives Holm. A2 FAILs only through the House joint test (t = -4.0, p = 0.0055). Senate rates (3.26-5.25%) are inside the Senate prediction interval [2.52%, 15.94%] (joint p = 0.16). 117's Senate rate (3.26%) is still the lowest in the series, below the train minimum (3.68%, 111). A pooled rate hides a chamber-specific shift.
A-c15-txt.caveats: The FAIL depends on the joint test, which assumes 116, 117 and 118 are independent. They are consecutive, and 116-117 share a House-D majority, so the effective sample is smaller and the p-value is anti-conservative. The 117 House cell (t = -3.6) is large, but on its own it does not survive Holm. The Senate interval is wide, so a moderate Senate shift could go undetected. The House drop coincides with the House label-miss shift in A1b (House unrep_share 0.587-0.593 in 116-117), so part of it is plausibly the same artifact.

A-c15-o1.interpretation: The chart shows the Task-2 rate per chamber, pooled, and under the alternative label. Train Congresses oscillate between about 4% and 9% with no monotone trend, peaking at 115. All series drop at 116 and bottom out at 117 (House 2.6%, pooled 2.8%), then recover partly in 118 (pooled 4.4%, about the level of 111-112). The alternative-label line sits above the main label throughout. Its 116-117 dip is proportionally shallower, as A1c shows, but it does not recover in 118.
A-c15-o1.caveats: The 115 to 116 step looks dramatic partly because 115 is the train maximum. For calibration, the gap that matters is the one to the pooled train mean (6.5%), and the one between the val and test Congresses (2.8% vs 4.4% for S1b).

A-c17-txt.interpretation: For Task 1, the eligible pool is the point-in-time roster of legislators in office (delegates included). The share of bills gaining at least one new cosponsor in (t0, t0+30] stays inside train (0.320-0.384 at t0 = 0; A3b PASS). New cosponsors per bill fall in 118, though: 1.47 at t0 = 0 against 2.19-2.97 in train, and 1.10 at t0 = 7. Positive density (positives / eligible) in 118 is 0.47% at t0 = 0 and 0.35% at t0 = 7. That is about 40% below the train mean (about 0.80% at t0 = 0) and about 68% of the train minimum. In prediction-interval-scaled distance on the log scale, t = -5.2 and -4.9. Both cells survive Holm and are labelled breaks (A3 FAIL). 117 is low but inside the interval (t = -2.0 and -2.2), and 116 is normal (t = +0.6 and +0.1). So the Task-1 break is specific to 118, and A3 fails for every split that evaluates 118 (S1b, S2, S3, S4, S1pool and stream variants) but not for S1a.
A-c17-txt.caveats: Censoring is small (2.2-3.9% in candidates) and similar in 117 and 118, so it does not explain the 118 drop. The legacy full-Congress denominator gives nearly identical densities, so the pool definition is not the cause either. For the mechanism, see A4 and A6: the evidence points more to dilution by bill volume than to a smaller pool of joiners.

A-c17-o1.interpretation: Density is roughly flat (about 0.7-0.9% at t0 = 0 and 0.55-0.75% at t0 = 7) from 108 to 116, then falls through 117 to 118. The t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 lines move in parallel, so the change is not specific to the first week after introduction.
A-c17-o1.caveats: Ranking metrics such as Recall@K and NDCG depend on how many positives each bill has. A lower density makes 118 harder for any model, so a raw score drop on 118 cannot be attributed to the model without a density-matched baseline (e.g. random and popularity rankers scored on the same Congress).

A-c19-txt.interpretation: The share of cosponsorships that are original (listed at introduction) is 0.330-0.394 in train, then 0.383 (116), 0.460 (117) and 0.466 (118). 117 and 118 are about 4 interval-scaled units above train (t = +3.8, +4.0). Both survive Holm and are labelled breaks (A4 FAIL). Cosponsors joining in days 1-30 fall from about 0.18-0.22 of all cosponsorships to 0.172 (117) and 0.141 (118). A higher original share is one possible contributor to the 118 density drop in A3, but not a sufficient explanation. 117 has almost the same original share as 118 (0.460 vs 0.466), yet its density stays inside the interval. These are also shares of total cosponsorships, which do not by themselves fix density per (bill, legislator) pair. A6 adds counts: 118 has 23,736 new day-1-30 cosponsorships, inside the train range (22,400-30,804), while its law-capable volume is 1.54x the mean train Congress. The more direct reading is that in 118 a normal number of joiners is spread over many more bills, the same dilution mechanism behind the Task-2 rate in 116 and 118.
A-c19-txt.caveats: Inference, not tested: whether the rise in original share reflects changed practice (e.g. assembling coalitions before introduction) or a recording change. A7's n_original PSI points the same way (ratio above 1 in all three candidates) but does not survive Holm. Either way, the input graph at t0 (more original-cosponsor edges) and the target both move, so t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 results should be reported separately.

A-c21-txt.interpretation: The pooled-chamber odds ratio (OR) for a majority-party sponsor's bill being reported is 1.96-3.72 in train, against 1.72 (116), 1.44 (117) and 2.48 (118). Only 117 is outside the interval (t = -2.8), and nothing survives Holm (A5 PASS). Conditioning on regime (which party controls the chamber) explains part of the dip. Between-Congress variance of the log OR is about 4x smaller within regime (tau^2 = 0.023) than within chamber with regime ignored (0.088), and no candidate cell differs significantly from same-regime train Congresses (A5b PASS, largest |z| = 1.70). All three House candidates still fall below their own regime reference (z = -1.70 for 116 House-D, -1.54 for 117 House-D, -1.23 for 118 House-R). That same-direction pattern suggests a residual House decline that this per-cell test cannot confirm. Within train, the majority effect is larger under R control than under D control, in the House (4.78 vs 2.38, z = -4.17) and in the Senate (2.38 vs 1.61, z = -2.40; A5c INFO).
A-c21-txt.caveats: A5b tests each cell alone against a reference with n = 2 for House-D (110, 111), so it has very little power. Its pass is weak evidence of a match. Party control is also partly confounded with era (both D-House train Congresses are 110-111).

A-c21-o1.interpretation: In the per-chamber ORs coloured by controlling party, R-controlled train Houses (108, 109, 112-115) cluster high (3.67-7.32) and D-controlled train Houses (110, 111) lower (2.87, 1.97). The candidate D-Houses 116 and 117 (1.64, 1.69) sit below both D-controlled train Houses. 118's R-controlled House (3.45) is higher than 116-117 but is the lowest R-controlled House in the series. The Senate is lower and flatter (1.16-3.19). So the regime pattern is real, but it does not account for the whole candidate decline. The concept looks regime-dependent, with a possible additional downward drift in the House that n = 2-6 reference Congresses per regime cannot resolve.
A-c21-o1.caveats: Several Senate confidence intervals include or approach 1 (e.g. 112 Senate 0.85-2.00, 117 Senate 0.83-1.62). Single-Congress Senate ORs are noisy.

A-c23-txt.interpretation: Among cosponsors joining in days 1-30, the share from the sponsor's party rose from 0.712 (108) to about 0.79-0.83 in 110-115. Candidates sit at 0.832, 0.860 and 0.832, inside the interval [0.676, 0.898] (A6 PASS; trend residuals near zero). The same-party prior a link predictor learns from train transfers, with at most a slight further rise in 117. The count row matters for A3. New day-1-30 cosponsorships number 36,895 (116), 30,200 (117) and 23,736 (118), against 22,400-30,804 in train. 118's count is ordinary even though its bill volume is 1.54x the train mean, which points to volume dilution as the main driver of its low density.
A-c23-txt.caveats: This is a marginal share. It does not show whether *which* cross-party members cosponsor changed, which A18 addresses partly. The count row is descriptive (no interval is computed for it), and it covers bills with a D/R sponsor only.

A-c25-txt.interpretation: Population stability index (PSI) measures how much one feature's distribution moved. Against pooled 108-115, no bill feature shows Holm-surviving drift (A7 PASS). Harmonised policy area has PSI 0.238-0.288 for candidates, against 0.035-0.272 for train Congresses left out one at a time (leave-one-out, LOO). Chamber, bill type and sponsor status are essentially unchanged (PSI at most 0.002). The only consistent signal is n_original (original-cosponsor count, PSI 0.079-0.114, joint p = 0.034, not Holm-surviving), which echoes A4. Without harmonisation, policy-area PSI is 0.357-0.436, inflated by taxonomy changes, and folding 4 unstable categories removes that. Law-capable bill volume is 14,340 / 15,242 / 16,565 against 8,621-11,414 in train. All three cells and the joint test (t = +5.9) survive Holm (A8 FAIL), so this is the one shift present in every candidate. 118 is labelled a break, and 116-117 are undetermined because the 108-115 slope is not significant.
A-c25-txt.caveats: The A7 reference spread is wide because 109 and 112 are themselves far from later Congresses (see the JSD heatmap), so a moderate policy-area shift would pass. The family-wise LOO false-alarm rate of 25% over 6 parts shows the raw per-part rule is noisy, which is why Holm is applied. Volume growth affects graph size (bill nodes per Congress) and dilutes both the Task-2 rate and Task-1 density.

A-c25-o1.interpretation: The chart divides each candidate's PSI by the largest train LOO PSI, so a bar above 1 means the candidate drifts more than any train Congress does from the others. Only n_original exceeds 1 in all three candidates (1.09, 1.14, 1.58, rising with time), and policy area just exceeds it in 118 (1.06). All other features sit far below 1.
A-c25-o1.caveats: A ratio just above 1, measured against the maximum of 8 values, is weak evidence on its own. Its weight comes from agreeing with A4.

A-c27-txt.interpretation: Each candidate's mean Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) of the policy-area mix to the train Congresses is 0.049-0.057. That sits inside the train LOO interval [0.024, 0.070] (A9 PASS). The Spearman correlation between Congress gap and JSD is 0.68 (A10 INFO, above the 0.5 threshold). Topic-mix drift is gradual, with nearby Congresses more alike than distant ones.
A-c27-txt.caveats: A10's correlation runs over all pairs of one matrix, so pairs are not independent. 0.68 describes the pattern; it is not a significance test.

A-c27-o0.interpretation: The heatmap has a clear block structure. Congresses 113-118 are nearly identical in policy-area mix (pairwise JSD 0.002-0.023). 108-111 are moderately distant from them (about 0.035-0.067), and 109 and 112 are far from 113-118 (0.089-0.113). They are close to their own neighbours, though (109 vs 110 0.013, 109 vs 111 0.029, 112 vs 111 0.022). So the real structure is a boundary between 112 and 113, not two isolated outliers. For the candidates, the nearest training Congresses are 113-115, not the full 108-115 pool.
A-c27-o0.caveats: Hypothesis, not tested here: the sharp 112 to 113 boundary may reflect a change in how policy areas were coded or harmonised rather than a change in agenda. Either way, the pre-113 Congresses widen the reference spread used by A7/A9/A11 and make those checks more lenient.

A-c29-txt.interpretation: A domain classifier (logistic regression on bill features, 2-fold cross-validated) separates each candidate's bills from the 108-115 pool with AUROC 0.629 / 0.630 / 0.646. Train Congresses separate from the other seven with AUROC 0.586-0.669, so the candidates are not unusual (A11 PASS). Without policy area (the t0-safe set), candidate AUROCs are 0.584-0.591 against 0.542-0.668. No joint covariate shift beyond normal between-Congress variation is detectable. The top separating coefficients are an (unstable/missing) policy-area bucket, Foreign Trade and International Finance (about -1.8 to -2.2 log-odds in all three), and, in 117, the 11 caucus-less sponsors (+3.10). The first and last are plausibly bookkeeping effects. Whether the Foreign Trade coefficient is a coding change or a real topic shift is a hypothesis the notebook does not test.
A-c29-txt.caveats: An AUROC of 0.6-0.65 for every Congress, train included, means Congresses are always somewhat distinguishable. The test shows the candidates are no *more* distinct than usual, not that they are identical to train. A linear classifier cannot detect nonlinear or graph-structural shift. Section B covers graph structure.

A-c31-txt.interpretation: In a forward-chained logistic Task-2 model (Congress c scored by a model fitted on 108..c-1), calibration-in-the-large (OE, observed / predicted rate) is 0.62, 0.47 and 0.73 on the candidates, so the model over-predicts, as A1 implies. Train forward folds also swing widely (OE 0.70-1.46), so base-rate miscalibration from one Congress to the next is normal, not new. The calibration slope is 0.675 / 0.791 / 0.621 (over-confident), inside the wide 6-Congress interval [0.613, 1.176] (A12 PASS; joint p = 0.039, not Holm). Discrimination drops. Forward AUROC is 0.666 / 0.674 / 0.664 against 0.712-0.781 for train folds. With t0-safe features only, it is 0.562 / 0.558 / 0.599 against 0.620-0.681 (A13 FAIL). Evidence strength differs by part. auroc_noPA has Holm-surviving cells for 116 and 117. The full auroc and the 118 noPA value fail only through joint tests (t = -4.6 and -5.0). Whether the majority-coefficient shift drives this cannot be resolved here: the coef_shift interval [-1.527, 0.819] is wider than 2 log-odds, and the majority OR did fall in 116-117 (A5: 1.72, 1.44), which plausibly explains part of their AUROC loss. 118's normal majority OR (2.48) next to a low AUROC suggests the majority effect is not the whole story.
A-c31-txt.caveats: The joint tests treat 116-118 as independent, so their p-values are optimistic. The consistency of the drop (all six candidate values below the train minimum) is still hard to attribute to chance. The reference is 6 forward folds, each fitted on fewer Congresses than the candidates' models, which if anything favours the candidates. The leave-one-out columns show the same drop (0.661-0.678), so it is not an artifact of the forward protocol. This is a linear model with bill features only, and a GNN using cosponsor-graph signals may degrade differently. Inference, not tested: the AUROC drop together with volume growth fits an influx of low-probability bills that look ordinary on these features.

A-c33-txt.interpretation: Per-Congress logistic fits on sampled (bill, legislator) pairs at t0 = 7 give coefficients for five pair features: sponsor-to-legislator cosponsor history, reciprocity, legislator activity, same caucus and same state. Two raw failures appear, both breaks: history in 116 (0.416 vs 0.507-0.723) and same_state in 117 (0.370 vs 0.521-0.897). Neither survives Holm over 15 cells plus 5 joint tests (A18 PASS; 7 reference Congresses, 109-115). The only directional hint is same_caucus, higher in 116-118 (1.19-1.36 vs 0.67-1.15; joint p = 0.039, not Holm), which agrees with A6. A forward-chained pair model gets pooled-pair AUROC 0.718 / 0.730 / 0.751 on 116-118. 116 is inside the train-fold range (0.703-0.724), and 117-118 are above it. Calibration slope is 0.98-1.14 (A18b PASS). So the pair-level discrimination of a simple model does not degrade at t0 = 7. 118's t = +4.3 is a distribution change in its own right, even though its direction is favourable.
A-c33-txt.caveats: The family-wise LOO false-alarm rate of the coefficient checks is 43% over 5 parts, so single-coefficient deviations are expected and the two raw breaks should not be over-read. A18b is a pooled-pair AUROC with negatives subsampled to 10%, from a 5-feature model at t0 = 7 only. It is not per-bill Recall@K/NDCG, and t0 = 0 is not tested. 118's higher AUROC coincides with the density drop (A3) and a higher same_caucus coefficient. It may reflect a change in the composition of positives (fewer, more predictable joiners) rather than a stable relationship, and per-bill ranking scores can still fall on 118.

A-c33-o1.interpretation: The coefficient trajectories are mostly noisy flat bands. History stays around 0.4-0.7. Reciprocity fluctuates around zero (-0.199 to +0.124) and changes sign across Congresses. Activity is mostly 0-0.2, with sign flips in 108 (-0.093) and 112 (-0.015) and a high of 0.444 in 109. Same_caucus drifts up from about 0.7-1.15 in train to 1.19-1.36 in 116-118. Same_state is 0.52-0.90 apart from 117's dip (0.37). The near-zero features changing sign is expected noise, not a concept reversal. The features with clearly non-zero effects (history, same_caucus, same_state) keep their sign throughout.
A-c33-o1.caveats: The coefficients are per unit on different scales (log1p counts vs binary indicators), so their raw sizes are not an importance ranking. 108 is shown but excluded from the reference because its 730-day look-back starts before the data.

A-c35-txt.interpretation: A14 measures, for each split and role, how far each evaluation unit's training pool is from the Congress it evaluates. It uses four distances: domain AUROC, |log| advancement-rate ratio (adv_logratio), |log| cosponsor-density ratio (dens_logratio) and topic JSD. The S1 rows matter most for the val/test choice, and they show a task-specific mismatch. S1a validates on 116, whose Task-1 density is almost identical to its pool (0.012), and tests on 117, which has the largest Task-2 rate gap of any unit (0.786). S1b validates on 117 (the same 0.786 Task-2 gap) and tests on 118, which has the largest Task-1 density gap (0.591) but a small Task-2 gap (0.259). So in S1a, Task-2 model selection happens on a near-normal Congress and is scored on the outlier. In S1b, Task-2 selection and any recalibration happen on the outlier, and Task 1 is scored on its outlier. For S2 vs S3 test units, sliding window S2 (k = 3) has lower mean domain AUROC (0.622 vs 0.631), density gap (0.182 vs 0.214) and topic JSD (0.024 vs 0.040), and a slightly larger rate gap (0.385 vs 0.354). It is closer in 18 of 28 fold x metric comparisons (A14 INFO 0.6429).
A-c35-txt.caveats: This is a distribution proxy, not performance. A 3-Congress pool has far fewer examples, and section D's backtest decides the trade-off. S2/S3 mean differences are small (about 0.01 in domain AUROC), and the 28 comparisons are not independent. Each S1 row is a single Congress, so its distances describe that Congress, not a typical one.

A-c35-o1.interpretation: Per test fold, the sliding pool is less distinguishable from its test Congress in 115, 117 and 118 (e.g. 0.561 vs 0.611 in 117, 0.574 vs 0.624 in 118). The expanding pool is closer in 112-114 and 116. On domain AUROC alone, sliding wins only 3 of 7 folds, but its advantage is largest in the most recent folds.
A-c35-o1.caveats: Fold-level domain AUROCs carry 2-fold cross-validation noise. Differences of a few hundredths in one fold are within the train LOO spread seen in A11.

A-c37-txt.interpretation: The in-progress 119th Congress (16,947 law-capable bills, days 0-650) is compared with each earlier Congress over the same day window, on t0-safe features without party-encoding columns. The least distinguishable are 115 (0.539), 116 (0.541), 118 (0.548) and 113 (0.549). 117 is at 0.559, and 109 and 112 are most distinct (0.608, 0.621). 119's distances to 113-118 (0.539-0.559) are all slightly above the median consecutive-pair distance (0.536) but well below its maximum (0.621). 119 vs pooled 108-117 is 0.552. So 119 looks like an ordinary next Congress. Of the two candidate test Congresses, 118 (S1b) is a marginally better deployment proxy than 117 (S1a) (0.548 vs 0.559). Per-feature PSIs of 119 vs 118 are all small (at most 0.049). Adding sponsor caucus and majority status makes same-regime Congresses (114, 115) look closest by construction, because the D-sponsored share follows the majority (0.48 in 119, 114-115 and 118).
A-c37-txt.caveats: A15 uses bill features only and cannot see the outcome shifts that matter most (A1-A4, A13). 119's labels are mostly censored, so whether it resembles 116-117 (Task-2 break) or 118 (Task-1 break) on outcomes is unknown. A 0.011 AUROC difference between 117 and 118 is small relative to the fold noise in A14.

A-c37-o1.interpretation: The no-party line (119 vs each Congress) is low and fairly flat from 113 onward (0.539-0.559) and higher for 108-112. The with-party line equals the no-party line for Congresses that share 119's RH/RS regime (108, 109, 114, 115). It is raised for every Congress with a different regime, most strongly for 110-113 and 116 (0.643-0.713, including the R-House/D-Senate Congresses 112 and 113), and less for 117-118 (0.600, 0.561). The consecutive-pair line gives the usual Congress-to-Congress distance (0.525-0.621). 119's distance to recent Congresses is slightly above the median and well within the range of consecutive steps.
A-c37-o1.caveats: The with-party line mostly reflects how the regime determines sponsor-party shares. It should not be read as substantive similarity (see A15b).

A-c39-txt.interpretation: A regression over all 66 Congress pairs (AUROC ~ gap + [gap = 1] + same_regime, with permutation p-values) separates time distance from shared party control. With party-encoding features removed, sharing a regime has essentially no effect (b = -0.0035, p_perm = 0.30). Time gap has a small positive effect at the edge of significance (b = 0.0034 per Congress, p = 0.056). Adding the majority flag gives b_same = -0.013 (p = 0.098). Only when sponsor caucus is included does regime become strongly significant (b = -0.062, p = 0.002), which is the by-construction effect. In bill-feature space, the evidence favours weak recency over regime. 115 is the closest Congress to 119 under every feature set.
A-c39-txt.caveats: This proxy uses bill composition only. A5/A5c show that regime does matter for the *outcome relationship* (majority-sponsor OR), which this test cannot see. Regime belongs in the model as a feature or interaction, but these data give no basis for selecting or weighting training Congresses by regime. Section D's D26 is the outcome-based test. With 12 Congresses and 4/11 consecutive pairs sharing a regime, power is limited.

A-c39-o1.interpretation: The pairwise no-party heatmap shows that 113-119 form a tight cluster (most pairwise AUROCs about 0.53-0.56). 109 and especially 112 are distinct from everyone (often 0.60-0.64), and 108-111 are moderately separated from the recent block. Labels with the same House/Senate majority do not visibly cluster once party features are removed, which agrees with the null regime coefficient in A15b.
A-c39-o1.caveats: Pairwise AUROCs share Congresses, so cells are strongly dependent. Visual clusters should not be read as independent confirmations.

A-c41-txt.interpretation: Section summary: 13 pass, 6 fail, 5 info. Holm survivors, with the evidence type: 116: A1b (cell + joint), A2 House (joint only), A8 (cell + joint), A13 auroc (joint only), A13 auroc_noPA (cell + joint). 117: the same plus A4 (cell + joint). 118: A3 at both t0 (cells), A4 (cell + joint), A8 (cell + joint), A13 auroc and auroc_noPA (joint only, confirming raw cell failures). So the Task-2 base-rate and label-validity clusters fail for 116-117 but not 118, and the Task-1 label cluster fails for 117 (A4) and 118 (A3, A4). Candidates fail 4/6, 5/6 and 3/6 clusters against 0.89 expected (Poisson-binomial p = 0.005, <0.001, 0.044), so A17 FAILs. Two thirds of the failing level parts are labelled breaks (A16 metric 0.667). The rest are undetermined because the train slope is not significant, and none is a predictable trend. S1a and S1a+stream fail 6 of 20 judged checks and the other forward splits 7, the difference being A3 (118 only). S5 is judged on 0 checks.
A-c41-txt.caveats: Three layers of approximation: (1) joint tests treat 116-118 as independent although they are consecutive and partly share regimes; (2) the cluster false-alarm model 1 - 0.95^m assumes roughly independent clusters, although A1b and A2 House are linked; (3) trend-vs-break labels come from a linear fit on 8 points extrapolated 1-3 steps, so 'break' does not rule out a nonlinear trend. 118's A17 result (p = 0.044) is borderline, and its Task-2 concept cluster rests on joint tests only. Near-identical failure counts across forward splits mean the counts do not discriminate between forward splits. The per-Congress pattern does.

A-c41-o1.interpretation: The heatmap of t (candidate vs train, in prediction-interval-scaled units) shows the per-Congress pattern. Task-2 rows (A1, A2 House, A1b) are most extreme in 116-117 and much milder in 118 (e.g. A1b +2.7 / +2.4 / +0.7; A2 House -2.4 / -3.6 / -1.6). The Task-1 density rows are extreme only in 118 (-5.2, -4.9; 116 at +0.6). Original share is high in 117-118 (+3.8, +4.0). Covariate rows (PSI, JSD, domain AUROC) are mostly near zero, as are A3b and A6. A1c and A5 are moderately negative across candidates without individual failures.
A-c41-o1.caveats: For one-sided distance checks such as PSI, a large negative t (e.g. A7 ch 117 at -4.5) means *less* drift than train, not a failure. The colour scale treats both directions symmetrically.

implications: Use a forward, by-Congress split, and treat S5 (random) only as a leakage reference. The shifts found here (volume and Task-2 AUROC in all candidates, Task-2 rate and label validity in 116-117, Task-1 density in 118) are differences between history and the deployment period that only a forward split measures. Section A's failure counts barely discriminate between forward splits (6 vs 7 of 20).

The val/test choice is task-specific. 116-117 are the Task-2 break Congresses (label-miss share 60.5% / 58.1%, House rate t = -2.4 / -3.6), and 118 partly reverts on Task 2 but breaks on Task-1 density. S1a (val 116, test 117) *tests* Task 2 on its most anomalous Congress (A14 rate gap 0.786). S1b (val 117, test 118) *validates* Task 2 on that same Congress and tests Task 1 on the density outlier (gap 0.591). 118 is only marginally closer to 119 (domain AUROC 0.548 vs 0.559). Neither single pair is clean, so report each task per Congress (116, 117, 118). Prefer rolling-origin evaluation across 116-118 to a single test Congress, letting no one Congress's anomaly dominate the conclusion.

Task 2 calibration: forward OE is 0.47-0.73 on candidates, but train folds also swing (0.70-1.46). Recalibrating the intercept on the val Congress alone is not supported by section A. In S1b, carrying over 117's level (2.8%, OE 0.47) to 118 (4.4%, OE 0.73) would under-predict by roughly 1.5x. Treat recalibration as a choice to test out of sample (section D's backtest), or base it on pooled recent Congresses. Select models with base-rate-insensitive metrics (AUROC). Report AP together with each test Congress's prevalence (or AP / prevalence), and report House and Senate separately.

Task 2 label: report the alternative label (reported OR passed origin chamber within 180 days) as a sensitivity analysis. In 116-117, 58-61% of chamber-passed bills have no committee report within 180 days (35-53% in train; 47% in 118), so in those Congresses the main label penalises correctly ranked bills that advanced by other routes.

Task 1: compare Recall@K/NDCG against per-Congress baselines (random, popularity, same-party heuristics), stratify by number of positives, and report t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 separately. 118's density is about 40% below the train mean (0.47% vs about 0.80% at t0 = 0), apparently because a normal number of joiners (23,736) is spread over 1.54x more bills. So raw score drops on 118 partly reflect task difficulty, not model failure. A simple pair model's pooled-pair AUROC (t0 = 7) does not degrade, but that does not guarantee stable per-bill ranking scores.

Model design: add chamber-control (regime) features and a sponsor-majority x controlling-party interaction. Within train, the House majority OR is 4.78 under R vs 2.38 under D (z = -4.17). Regime alone does not close the gap: all three House candidates sit below their regime reference (z = -1.2 to -1.7). Do not select or weight training Congresses by regime on bill-feature similarity, because A15b finds no regime effect once party-encoding features are removed.

Consider recency weighting or a shorter window as a tuned option, not a default. Recent pools are modestly closer to their test Congress (S2 closer in 18/28 comparisons; 113-118 form a tight topic-mix block). Let section D's backtest decide, given the smaller sample. Include bill-volume-sensitive and t0-dependent features such as original-cosponsor count, whose distribution is shifting upward (A4, A7 n_original).
open_questions: Is the 116-118 drop in Task-2 discriminability (forward AUROC 0.664-0.674 vs 0.712-0.781) a property of the bills (e.g. more low-probability bills inflating volume), of the majority effect weakening in 116-117, or of the simple feature set? Section A cannot tell whether a graph model using cosponsor-network signals would recover it.

Will 119 resemble 116-117 (Task-2 label/rate break) or 118 (Task-1 density break and Task-2 reversion)? Its outcomes are still censored. 116-117 overlap COVID-era procedural changes, and 118 is a single Congress, so neither pattern can yet be called lasting.

Several passes (A1, A1c, A5, A12 slope, A7 n_original, A18 same_caucus) show same-direction deviations across candidates with nominal joint p < 0.05 that do not survive Holm. With 6-8 reference Congresses and autocorrelated candidates, these may be real but small shifts or chance.

Is the sharp 112 to 113 boundary in policy-area mix a coding or harmonisation artifact? If so, the reference spreads for A7/A9/A11 are inflated and the covariate-stability passes are more lenient than they appear.
